html:
I had barely heard of Jia Zhangke. Until a Zhihu recommendation a couple of days ago, I had only a vague impression of the name and had never seen any of his films. Once I’d been filled in, I learned that he belongs to the so-called “Sixth Generation” of Chinese directors, that almost half his films can’t be shown in mainland China, that he is better known abroad than at home, and that he excels at portraying society and life as they really are.

On Friday, by the time I’d finished work and had dinner, it was already ten o’clock, and I went looking for a film. On Douban, Ash Is Purest White (Chinese title Jianghu ernü, “Sons and Daughters of the Jianghu”) was rated 7.7, and Duonao, a streaming site, to my surprise already had a proper copy rather than a camcorder rip (the film had only been out in China for a week). Marveling at Duonao’s conscientiousness, I pressed play.

The Chinese films I like fall into two kinds. One is historical, set more than 150 years ago, with no trace of the present on screen: partly because history is appealing, and partly for the fun of searching for things in it that mirror life today. The other is recent films, from the 1980s to now, the years I’ve lived through, where my mind fills in the picture on its own. The well-made ones (made with care but without extravagance, acted with sincerity but without big stars) always touch something in you at certain moments, perhaps through some object that evokes its era, a line of dialogue, or a hairstyle stamped with its time.

From its very first scene, Ash Is Purest White transported me straight back to 2001, my first year of junior high. The picture is shaky and grayish. A crowd of working people sit on a bus: vacant eyes, clothes in drab colors, skin weathered by life, and a chubby little girl with earrings, short hair and overalls. Without a doubt, this is what a small Chinese city looked like at the start of the 21st century.

Shanxi. In my childhood it seemed to lie at the far end of the earth, simply because my uncle lived there and hadn’t been home in decades. Our only contact was a phone call every few months, which convinced me it was a million miles away; I couldn’t imagine what it looked like. This film gave me the answer: exactly like my hometown.

Apart from the few with distinctive landmarks, Chinese cities are hard to tell apart. In one such run-down, remote city lives a band of rather colorful gangsters. They’re nothing like the ones in Hong Kong films: not handsome in the least, not obviously rich, speaking a dialect in which “you” and “me” sound alike, crammed into a cramped little “casino,” smoking up a storm, chatting and laughing. If a gun hadn’t fallen out and given them away, I’d have believed they were miners. Among these Shanxi gangsters is a woman who moves between the jianghu, the underworld with its own code of loyalty, and ordinary life. She is fairly attractive, not especially good and certainly not bad, and flirts with Brother Bin’s men while knowing exactly where to draw the line.

The first twenty-odd minutes are a little slow, until Second Brother’s death. The gang’s boss is dead and the gang is leaderless; everyone is burning with fury to avenge him, yet in the end that scene never comes. It’s like a replay of the “Brother Long” meme that swept the Chinese internet: while Brother Long lived, “Brothers united, our strength can cut through metal!”; when Brother Long got hacked, “Hang in there, bro, I’ve got to run!”; after Brother Long died, “Farewell, big brother, in eighteen years you’ll be back a hero!”

After Second Brother’s death, the gang changes a great deal. Its real-estate business gets squeezed out, Brother Bin is beaten up twice, and then come Qiaoqiao’s two gunshots: the 2001 section is over. According to Wikipedia, these were the big events in China that year:

January 10: Shenzhou 2 lifts off.

January 23: the “zf” incident.

April 1: the pilot Wang Wei goes missing after his fighter jet collides with a US surveillance plane.

July 1: the important thought of the “Three Represents.”

July 13: Beijing wins the right to host the 2008 Olympics.

September to October: a series of match-fixing scandals hits Jia B, China’s second-tier football league, later known as the “Jia B Five Rats” affair.

October 7: China’s national football team qualifies for the World Cup finals for the first time.

October 21: China’s railways carry out their fourth major speed-up, covering nearly all the larger cities and most regions of the country.

November 11 to 25: Guangzhou hosts the 9th National Games.

December: China joins the World Trade Organization.

Anyone born before 1990 should remember many of these vividly, and I’m convinced that’s why Jia chose 2001. Winning the Olympics and reaching the World Cup won China a huge amount of attention in Asia and around the world, while the economy took off for good, charging toward becoming the world’s second-largest. Nobody could have guessed that a few years later, Second Brother’s unfinished property development would become the most lucrative business of all: owning a mine was nothing compared with owning real estate. Qiaoqiao, meanwhile, sitting in prison for her man, missed five years of rapid change on the outside, and got her first color-screen phone the moment she came out.

Five years later, Qiaoqiao is released, and the city seems to have shifted into a higher gear: buildings going up at a frantic pace, the Three Gorges Dam project uprooting so many people from their homes. Once again, unmistakable marks of that era. Against this backdrop come all the things we love to watch: kept mistresses, wedding-banquet crashing, street performers with flashy salon-boy hair, and that song, sung to pieces but a pop tune that belonged to its era and perfectly expresses Qiaoqiao’s state of mind at the time: “How Much Love Can Start Over.”

She is, after all, a woman who ran with a gang boss. After a series of darkly comic scenes, crashing wedding banquets, conning people out of money, stealing a set of wheels, using the police to track down Brother Bin, you can’t help admiring her ability to survive. Just out of prison (when Ding Jiali walks into the ferry cabin, Qiaoqiao stands up out of habit), facing the betrayal of the boyfriend she once loved deeply and went to prison for, and a blank future, she doesn’t scream or sob or wail, doesn’t glare wide-eyed. There are only a few brief moments of red-rimmed eyes, still defiant, and they make a perfect portrait of a strong woman. These scenes, realistic and finely observed, and Zhao Tao’s explosive performance deliver something that goes straight to the heart, with no need for translation or much guesswork.

Time flows on, and in the blink of an eye it’s 2018. In an empty square: Brother Bin in a wheelchair, his expression as stubborn as ever; Qiaoqiao, a smartly dressed middle-aged woman now, her eyes wet but still defiant; and their long, stretched-out shadows. Together they lay out plainly everything that has changed over these years.

So much has changed: the two people’s ages and states of mind, the tower blocks that have shot up, the phones everyone uses. Yet a lot hasn’t: the furnishings of the mahjong parlor, the patch of wasteland where Qiaoqiao fired the gun and where Brother Bin practiced walking, and, deep in Qiaoqiao’s heart, her feelings for Brother Bin.

The plot itself isn’t especially original. A stubborn gang boss, to save face, never visits the girlfriend who went to prison for him, and betrays her. Down and out, in a wheelchair, he comes back to her, still clinging to and guarding the pitiful scrap of dignity he has cultivated over the years and kept, selectively, to the end. And that scrap of dignity won’t let him swallow his pride to secure the story a happy ending, so in the end he chooses to leave, leaving behind what may be the last few hundred-yuan notes he owns. No vows to love until the seas run dry, no tearful partings at death’s door: what Jia Zhangke shows us is life’s helplessness, and the disappointments life so often hands us, whether for face, for love, for loyalty, for money, whatever. You can tell the director wants to tell the audience a great deal, about the times, about human nature, about life. The ending is open. We don’t know what happens to Brother Bin and Qiaoqiao afterward, or what kind of lives they led during those seventeen years, and the film doesn’t say much about why Brother Bin deliberately keeps away from Qiaoqiao.

And isn’t that fine? Sometimes we don’t fully know what each step we take means either, and can’t give a standard answer.

In the jianghu, no one is master of their fate; the generations turn, and love runs long in its sons and daughters.
